summary: A consultant-level comparison of the 2023 ERS/ESICM/ESCMID/ALAT severe CAP guideline with the 2019 ATS/IDSA guideline, the 2025 ATS-only update (which IDSA declined to endorse) and NICE NG250 (September 2025, replacing NG138 and CG191; BTS remains 2009 with a 2015 annotated update). The European panel prefers a macrolide, not a fluoroquinolone, as the beta-lactam partner, based on observational data; ACCESS (2024) shows clarithromycin improves a surrogate early-response endpoint in ward patients, and a 2025 network meta-analysis finds no regimen convincingly superior. Guidelines converge on covering MRSA and Pseudomonas only when there are validated risk factors, using nasal MRSA PCR and cultures to de-escalate. Multiplex PCR speeds escalation but not de-escalation in the one large RCT. Steroids are covered briefly (CAPE COD positive, REMAP-CAP hydrocortisone stopped for futility; NICE 2025 now says consider a steroid). The main news is REMAP-CAP's influenza antiviral domain (preprint, 2026): in 442 critically ill patients, oseltamivir for 5 or 10 days was associated with higher 90-day mortality than no antiviral, which challenges every current guideline. Duration: 5 days per NICE, at least 5 per ATS 2025, with procalcitonin to shorten per ERS. BALANCE supports 7 rather than 14 days in bacteraemia.
takeaways: Beta-lactam plus macrolide is the default in severe CAP; keep levofloxacin for true penicillin allergy and be careful combining it with steroids (MHRA).
Cover MRSA or Pseudomonas only with prior respiratory isolation or recent admission with IV antibiotics, and use nasal MRSA PCR and cultures to de-escalate quickly.
Rapid multiplex panels only help if someone acts on the result the same day: in the RCT they sped up escalation, not de-escalation.
Oseltamivir is no longer automatic in ventilated or shocked influenza after REMAP-CAP (preprint): discuss with microbiology and recruit to trials.
Five to seven days of antibiotics for most patients, guided by clinical stability and procalcitonin.
